question: Can a minuet carry the mood of the movement before it?
intro: After the C minor Adagio, which ends on a held G and the word attacca, Haydn goes straight into a C major minuet. Its Trio turns back to C minor, and a rising scale closes the Menuetto each time.

sections.label: Menuetto da capo
sections.mNote: da capo: the Menuetto returns after the Trio

cues.title: Without a pause
cues.text: The Menuetto follows the Adagio’s final held G without a break, a bold move Shulman calls telescoping the two central movements into one. The key turns back to C major; the marking is Menuetto, Allegretto.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s note describes the movement as following the Adagio without pause; the score (IMSLP #05812, p. 191) is headed Menuetto, Allegretto, in C major with no flats. The report reads C major at 0:00–0:10 (r 0.87–0.90); this file starts at its own beginning, so the join to the Adagio is not in the audio.

cues.title: The second strain, in G
cues.text: The first strain, eight bars played twice, has led from C major to G major. At about 0:16 the second strain begins in G, the dominant, and the key estimate stays there for the next stretch.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 0:16 (novelty 0.75) is followed by a local-key estimate of G major at 0:15–0:30 (r 0.84–0.96). The score (IMSLP #05812, p. 191) puts a repeat sign after bar 8; the timing of the repeat is inferred from the 15.5 s length of the first section and is not aligned to bars.

cues.title: The second strain again
cues.text: At about 0:52 the second strain starts over, as its repeat sign requires. The loudest windows of the Menuetto fall in this second pass, so listen for the same phrases returning with the accented chords now more prominent.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 15.5–52.5 s with 53.5–90.5 s (mean chroma similarity 0.97, no transposition), and a boundary falls at 0:52 (0.47). The loudest windows include 0:50 (−11.6 dB) and 1:00. The score marks repeats at the end of both strains; the analysis is not a bar-level alignment.

cues.title: The Trio turns to C minor
cues.text: The Menuetto ends with rising scales in all four parts, a crescendo to fortissimo and a final chord, marked Fine. Then the Trio begins in C minor, as in the Adagio, with Shulman’s “unison melody” and tense augmented chords.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:30 (novelty 1.00), with the local key moving to C minor (r 0.59–0.67) at 1:35–1:50. The score shows rising scales with crescendo and ff, then Fine, then a change to three flats and Trio; Shulman describes the Trio’s unison melody and augmented chords.

cues.title: Not the first time
cues.text: Playing the Menuetto and slow movement as one is unusual but not new in Haydn’s quartets: Shulman points to an earlier example in Op. 20 No. 2. The Trio’s C minor and some of its musical material also tie it back to the Adagio.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s programme note (https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf) cites Op. 20 No. 2 as the precedent and says the Trio’s material is subtly linked to the Adagio.

cues.title: Swell and fade, in pairs
cues.text: In the second half of the Trio the score pairs forte with piano: each loud chord is followed by a fade. Listen for that rhythm of strike and fade, now in C minor, now touching G.
cues.evidence: Local key reads C minor at 2:05–2:25 (r 0.71–0.86) with G major at 1:55–2:00 and 2:25; boundaries at 1:52 (0.93) and 2:04 (0.56). The score’s f and p marks with fading hairpins in the Trio’s second part (IMSLP #05812, p. 192) support the description; bars are not aligned.

cues.title: Da capo
cues.text: At about 2:30 the Menuetto begins again, as the direction Menuetto D.C. at the end of the Trio requires. The quartet plays it through without the repeats, so the return lasts about fifty seconds, against about ninety for its first appearance.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 2:30 (novelty 0.93) with a second at 2:34 (0.95), and a local key of C major at 2:30–2:35 after the Trio’s C minor; a Trio path in the recurrence analysis runs to about 149.5 s. The recurrence lag of 144 s between 9.5–53.0 s and 153.5–197.0 s relates two excerpts and is not itself the onset of the return. The score ends the Trio with Menuetto D.C.; the first bar is not aligned.

cues.title: A slow finale to come
cues.text: The quartet’s last movement will not be the brisk, witty finale of convention: Shulman notes that Haydn opens it with another Adagio, and the music turns back to the Adagio’s gravity once more.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s note describes the finale as “another Adagio” varied by a Presto middle section. The recording ends near 3:20 (−15.6 dB at 3:15); this cue looks ahead to the next movement rather than describing sound at 3:06.

transitions.title: A rising scale, then C minor
transitions.how: The Menuetto’s second strain ends with rising scales in all four parts, a crescendo from forte to fortissimo and firm C major chords, marked Fine. The Trio then begins in the parallel minor, C minor, in a new three-flat key signature, with the four instruments in unison. The jump from loud major chords to a unison minor melody is what the ear takes as the join; no pivot chord softens it.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary is 1:30 (1.00); local keys read C major at 1:20–1:25 and C minor from 1:35. The score shows the scales with crescendo to ff, the word Fine, and the change to three flats; the unison is visible in the first bars of the Trio. Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: The Trio hands back to the Menuetto
transitions.how: The Trio’s second part ends in C minor, and the score’s direction Menuetto D.C. sends the players back to the beginning. The key signature returns to C major with no flats, so the opening Allegretto is restored without any transition passage: the join is a change of mode and a change of character, from the Trio’s serious C minor to the Menuetto’s dance. The Menuetto ends at its Fine.
transitions.evidence: The report has boundaries at 2:30 (0.93) and 2:34 (0.95) with C major at 2:30–2:35, after a Trio path in the recurrence analysis that runs to about 149.5 s; the 144 s lag between 9.5–53.0 s and 153.5–197.0 s is a lag between excerpts, not the onset of the return. The score shows Menuetto D.C. at the end of the Trio and the C major key signature at the top of the Menuetto; the exact bar is not aligned.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
